title: A hymn in Gujri
hookLine: a crane flies far from her chicks; who feeds them?

cards: A crane lifts off from a marsh and flies a long way, leaving her chicks behind in the reeds. Who feeds them while she's gone? Who teaches them anything?
That question isn't from a nature program. It's from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Gujri, one that a Sikh praying the evening Rehras says aloud.
A small surprise: yesterday's raga belongs to the morning, yet some of its hymns are carried into the evening prayer.

teach.b: The hymn opens by talking to the mind, in plain English: why, mind, do you keep scheming and straining, when the Lord himself is already busy with your care? Then the pictures come.

teach.h: FOOD SET OUT IN THE ROCKS.
teach.b: In rocks and stones the Creator places living things, and sets their food in front of them. Then the crane.
She flies far away, her chicks are left behind, and no one is there to feed them or teach them to peck. Think about it in your mind, the hymn says. Who looks after them?
Guru Arjan isn't telling anyone to stop working; Sikh teaching prizes honest labor.
The target is the anxious part of the mind that plans every outcome as if everything rested on it, still running the numbers at two in the morning.
Against that, the hymn sets a slower trust: you do your part, and the care was there before you started. The same raga holds a very different voice.

teach.h: TRILOCHAN: WHAT FILLS THE MIND AT THE END?
teach.b: Bhagat Trilochan, one of the saints whose words the Gurus gathered into the Granth, asks a sharper question in Gujri: at the very end, what fills the mind?
Thoughts of wealth, of wife and sons, of a fine mansion, each one shapes what comes next, he says, and only the one who remembers the Lord goes free. Two voices, one raga.
One soothes an anxious mind; one wakes a distracted one.
Both bring it back to the same place: steady, unshowy devotion, pointed at what matters.

how: Guru Arjan's Gujri hymn about the anxious mind and the crane is part of the Rehras, the evening prayer Sikhs recite or sing at sunset; in kirtan it is sung in Raga Gujri.

games.q: what does “a hymn in gujri” mean?
o: the crane hymn and Trilochan's question, in Gujri
a lullaby sung to small children at bedtime
a hymn praising birds as holy creatures of God

games.q: who said what in gujri — tap the pairs.
p: why, mind, do you scheme and strain?
what fills the mind at the end?

s: Guru Arjan's hymn tells people to stop working
Sikh teaching prizes honest labor; the hymn speaks to the anxious, scheming mind.
a Gujri hymn is part of the evening Rehras
a raga tradition places in the morning has hymns carried into the evening prayer.
the Granth's Gujri section holds only the Gurus' words
Bhagat Trilochan's verse is there too.

games.q: the crane has flown far, and her chicks are alone in the reeds. who looks after them, by the hymn's account?
o: nobody, so they must fend for themselves.
the Lord, who cares for every creature.
the other cranes of the flock.
games.why: the hymn asks the mind to think about it: the same Creator who sets food before creatures in the rocks cares for the chicks too.

practice: Breathe out longer than you breathe in, find the plan your mind keeps rehearsing today, the email, the bill, the conversation, and picture setting it on the floor beside you; it'll still be there after.
For now, picture the crane's chicks in the reeds, fed by no effort of their own. If you pray, say Waheguru and let the worry rest there; if you don't, let your hands lie open.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Gujri. Guru Arjan's crane, flying far while her chicks are cared for, and Bhagat Trilochan asking what fills the mind at the end. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: devotion in gujri. One voice soothes the anxious mind, and one wakes the distracted one. That's today, done.
